definition: Composite portraiture (also known as composite photographs) is a technique invented by Sir Francis Galton in the 1880s after a suggestion by Herbert Spencer for registering photographs of human faces on the two eyes to create an "average" photograph of all those in the photographed group.
details: Spencer had suggested using onion paper and line drawings, but Galton devised a technique for multiple exposures on the same photographic plate. He noticed that these composite portraits were more attractive than any individual member, and this has generated a large body of research on human attractiveness and averageness one hundred years later. He also suggested in a Royal Society presentation in 1883 that the composites provided an interesting concrete representation of human ideal types and concepts. He discussed using the technique to investigate characteristics of common types of humanity, such as criminals. In his mind, it was an extension of the statistical techniques of averages and correlation. In this sense, it represents one of the first implementations of convolution factor analysis and neural networks in the understanding of knowledge representation in the human mind. Galton also suggested that the technique could be used for creating natural types of common objects. During the late 19th century, English psychometrician Sir Francis Galton attempted to define physiognomic characteristics of health, disease, beauty, and criminality, via a method of composite photography

explainer.lead: A composite portrait blends several face photographs by aligning their eyes and exposing them onto the same photographic plate, creating an “average” face for the group. Francis Galton developed the technique in the 1880s to make shared types and concepts visible, and his observations later helped inspire research on facial averageness and attractiveness.

tiers.eli5: Imagine tracing several faces on clear sheets, lining up their eyes, and looking through the whole stack: shared features build up while individual differences fade. Galton did something similar with repeated exposures on one photographic plate, hoping to see what a whole group had in common.
tiers.practitioner: In its original form, gather a set of portraits, register them using the two eyes, and make multiple exposures on one photographic plate. Keep group membership, alignment, and capture conditions consistent so the result reflects the intended comparison. Treat the composite as a visualization of shared appearance, not evidence that facial features reveal criminality, health, or other traits.
tiers.paperLevel: Given portraits P1, ..., Pn, the construction is C = Composite(Register_eyes(P1), ..., Register_eyes(Pn)), implemented by Galton as multiple exposures on one photographic plate. Sir Francis Galton developed the method in the 1880s after Herbert Spencer’s suggestion and discussed it in an 1883 Royal Society presentation as a concrete representation of ideal types and concepts, extending statistical averages and correlation. Its historical physiognomic aims do not establish valid inferences about health, disease, or criminality.

explainer.example: To investigate a proposed criminal type, Galton could take portraits of several people classified as criminals, align every pair of eyes, and expose all the portraits onto one plate. The result was a single blended face that he proposed examining for shared characteristics.

usedIn.name: Facial attractiveness research
usedIn.detail: Galton’s observation that composites could be more attractive than any individual member helped generate later research on averageness and attractiveness.

usedIn.name: Knowledge representation
usedIn.detail: Galton presented composites as concrete representations of human ideal types and concepts.

usedIn.name: Historical physiognomy
usedIn.detail: Galton attempted to characterize health, disease, beauty, and criminality through composite photography; these were his aims, not established diagnostic uses.

explainer.intuition: The technique is a visual analogue of averaging: align many examples so recurring features reinforce one another while individual differences blend together. The resulting face offers a concrete image of a proposed group type.
howItWorks: Gather portraits of the people in the intended group.
Align each photograph by registering it on the two eyes.
Expose the aligned photographs successively onto the same photographic plate.
Examine the blended image as an “average” portrait or proposed common type.
explainer.whyItMatters: Composite portraiture turned the statistical intuition of averaging across instances into a visible object, which Galton connected to ideal types, concepts, and correlation. His observation that composites could be more attractive than their individual members later generated a large body of research on human attractiveness and averageness.
misconceptions: It is not a collage: the portraits are aligned and superimposed, not arranged side by side.
It is not automatically a diagnosis: Galton’s aims concerning health and criminality do not validate those inferences.
It is not a guaranteed beauty filter: increased attractiveness was an observation that motivated later research, not a promised result for every group.
